people.summary: Urban III’s short papacy brought the conflict with Frederick Barbarossa close to another rupture. A Milanese whose family had suffered during imperial warfare, he opposed the growing union of German and Sicilian power. Disputes over bishops and coronations escalated into blocked communications and military pressure. He died in 1187 as the crusader states faced disaster in the East.
people.biography:
Uberto Crivelli became archbishop of Milan shortly before his election as pope in 1185 and retained that see. His experience of Frederick’s destruction of Milan gave an intensely personal background to a conflict also rooted in jurisdiction and territory. The marriage of Frederick’s son Henry to Constance, heiress of Sicily, threatened to surround papal lands with one dynastic power.

Urban refused the imperial request concerning Henry’s coronation and supported Folmar in the contested archbishopric of Trier against the emperor’s candidate. Frederick obstructed papal messengers across the Alps and exerted pressure in Italy. Urban sought support among German bishops but found them unwilling to abandon the emperor.

He was preparing stronger censures when the people of Verona resisted their publication within an imperial city. Leaving for Venice, he died at Ferrara in October 1187. The familiar story linking his death to news of Jerusalem’s fall is not securely established by the chronology. His legates also worked to stop warfare between England and France, illustrating activity beyond the imperial dispute.

actions.text: Defended his candidate for Trier and opposed imperial interference in ecclesiastical affairs.
Resisted the political consequences of the Henry–Constance marriage and the concentration of power around papal territory.
Used legates to help secure a truce between the English and French kings in 1187.

people.context: Sicily had long been both a papal fief and a counterweight to imperial power. Its prospective union with the Hohenstaufen made every apparently technical dispute over a bishop or coronation part of a wider struggle for security. Urban’s restricted access to communication also shows how geography and armed control could limit papal authority.

people.summary: Gregory VIII served for less than two months, but his response to the loss of Jerusalem helped set the Third Crusade in motion. Formerly Alberto di Morra, an experienced papal chancellor and diplomat, he sought peace among Christian rulers and Italian maritime cities. His programme joined military preparations to prayer, fasting and moral reform rather than treating the crisis as a purely strategic defeat.
people.biography:
Alberto came from Benevento and entered the cardinalate under Adrian IV. Alexander III entrusted him with important diplomatic work, including the investigation and settlement following Thomas Becket’s murder. As chancellor he acquired long experience of the papacy’s correspondence and legal administration before succeeding Urban III in October 1187.

The defeat at Hattin and the loss of Jerusalem transformed the priorities of his brief reign. Gregory urged penitence and a new expedition for the Holy Land. He also made conciliatory approaches toward Frederick Barbarossa, recognizing that another western quarrel would obstruct the response.

Naval transport required cooperation between Pisa and Genoa, whose rivalry threatened preparations. Gregory travelled to Pisa to promote peace and organize assistance, but died there in December 1187. The work of assembling the expedition passed to Clement III. His short tenure matters because it established a direction that a successor could develop, not because he personally led the armies that followed.

actions.text: Called for a penitential response and a new crusade after the catastrophe in the Holy Land.
Sought reconciliation with Frederick Barbarossa to reduce conflict within the western Christian powers.
Tried to reconcile Pisa and Genoa, whose ships were necessary for transporting crusaders and supplies.

people.context: The Third Crusade depended on monarchs, financiers, ports and fleets acting together. Gregory understood that Christian political rivalries could make a religious appeal ineffective. His career as chancellor and negotiator helps explain why his immediate response to an eastern military crisis included efforts at western reconciliation.

people.summary: Clement III restored a working relationship between the papacy and Rome’s communal government while organizing the Third Crusade. A Roman cardinal known as Paolo Scolari, he could return to the city through a treaty that balanced civic liberties and papal sovereignty. The death of William II of Sicily then confronted him with another threat: Henry VI’s claim to the southern kingdom.
people.biography:
Paolo Scolari, cardinal bishop of Palestrina, was elected at Pisa in December 1187. His Roman origins and conciliatory reputation encouraged negotiations with the city’s senate. The resulting agreement recognized papal sovereignty while preserving municipal institutions, allowing him to establish himself in the Lateran after years of papal displacement.

Clement continued Gregory VIII’s response to Jerusalem’s loss. Legates sought peace among rulers and coordinated preparations for the expedition associated with Frederick Barbarossa, Philip Augustus and Richard I. The undertaking’s resources were immense, but rivalries and setbacks made its outcome uncertain; Clement died before the capture of Acre.

William II’s death in 1189 reopened the Sicilian succession. Henry VI claimed through his wife Constance, while Clement supported Tancred. A ruler controlling both the empire and Sicily threatened the papacy’s territorial independence. Clement also intervened in contested episcopal elections and recognized the Scottish Church’s direct relationship to Rome rather than subjection to York. He died in 1191.

actions.text: Concluded a treaty with Rome’s commune, securing papal residence while recognizing civic liberties.
Organized the Third Crusade through legates, diplomacy and appeals for cooperation.
Supported Tancred against Henry VI in Sicily and upheld a distinct jurisdictional position for the Scottish Church.

people.context: Rome’s senate was an enduring institution, not a temporary disturbance that could simply be ignored. Clement’s settlement acknowledged that reality. Abroad, the crusade required peace among competing kings, while Sicily showed the danger of dynastic inheritance concentrating power on both sides of papal territory.

people.summary: Celestine III inherited the Third Crusade and an increasingly powerful Henry VI. Elected after decades as a cardinal, he crowned Henry emperor but struggled to prevent the empire’s union with Sicily. His cautious diplomacy contrasts with firmer intervention in royal marriages, especially the defence of Ingeborg of Denmark after Philip II of France rejected her.
people.biography:
Giacinto Bobone had been a cardinal for many years before his election in 1191. Still a deacon, he received priestly ordination and episcopal consecration before crowning Henry VI and Constance. The accession was overshadowed by the destruction of Tusculum, which Rome’s citizens demanded and imperial forces enabled. Papal participation in the resulting settlement cannot be detached from that violence.

Henry’s campaigns for Sicily and his imprisonment of Richard I placed Celestine under pressure. The pope pursued negotiation and censures cautiously, seeking to preserve papal rights without provoking a confrontation he could not win. Henry ultimately secured Sicily in 1194, creating the strategic concentration of power that earlier popes had feared.

Celestine defended the validity of Philip II’s marriage to Ingeborg against a divorce supported by French bishops. He continued to support crusading institutions and religious communities. Henry died in 1197, shortly before the pope’s own death in January 1198, leaving a child heir and a transformed political situation for Innocent III.

actions.text: Crowned Henry VI while trying to preserve papal rights against the emperor’s expansion into Sicily.
Pressed for redress over Richard I’s captivity, though his cautious response attracted criticism.
Rejected Philip II’s attempted repudiation of Ingeborg, asserting that royal power did not dissolve a valid marriage.

people.context: Crusading did not suspend rivalry among Christian rulers: a returning crusader king could become another ruler’s valuable prisoner. Henry’s control of Germany and Sicily also threatened the papacy’s freedom of action. Celestine’s restraint therefore arose within a severe imbalance of power, even when contemporaries and later historians judged it insufficient.

people.summary: Innocent III brought medieval papal authority to an exceptional reach. He intervened in royal successions, guarded the young Frederick II and summoned the Fourth Lateran Council, whose pastoral rules shaped everyday Catholic life. He also welcomed Francis’s new movement. His reign also brought crusading violence and discriminatory legislation against religious minorities.
people.biography:
Lothar of Segni studied theology and law before entering papal service. Elected in 1198, he acted quickly after Henry VI’s death to strengthen papal authority in Rome and central Italy. As guardian of Frederick, the child king of Sicily, he sought to protect both the heir and the papacy’s rights. In Germany he intervened in the rivalry between Philip of Swabia and Otto, later turning against Otto when imperial expansion threatened papal lands.

Innocent’s dealings with John of England began over the succession to Canterbury. Interdict and excommunication helped force John to accept Stephen Langton; John then held his kingdoms as papal fiefs. When the barons imposed Magna Carta, Innocent annulled it as an agreement extracted from his vassal under coercion. Papal defence of church freedom thus coexisted with opposition to a charter later celebrated for limiting royal power.

He called the Fourth Crusade, but its diversion culminated in the sack of Constantinople in 1204. He protested the diversion and violence, then accepted the resulting Latin political order. After his legate’s murder in southern France, he called the Albigensian Crusade, whose religious campaign also became a war of conquest. These outcomes reveal the limits of papal control over armies mobilized with spiritual authority.

At the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215, Innocent’s programme addressed doctrine, preaching, education, marriage and clerical conduct. It required annual confession and Easter communion, without inventing confession itself. The council also imposed discriminatory dress rules on Jews and Muslims. Alongside centralized legislation, Innocent welcomed Francis and his companions, supporting a renewal based on poverty and preaching. He died in 1216.

actions.text: Asserted papal authority in the imperial succession and in disputes with rulers including John and Philip II.
Convened the Fourth Lateran Council, establishing lasting pastoral requirements while also enacting coercive and discriminatory provisions.
Launched crusading initiatives whose diversion and violence exceeded his intended purposes and damaged Christian relations.
Welcomed Francis’s movement, giving ecclesiastical space to a new form of apostolic poverty.

people.context: Innocent understood papal office as a responsibility to judge grave sin and protect the Church across the Christian political order. That vision made royal marriage, warfare, succession and public religion matters for papal intervention. The same age’s hunger for evangelical poverty produced both movements condemned as heretical and communities welcomed within the Church, making his choices influential far beyond diplomatic affairs.

people.summary: Honorius III consolidated the new mendicant orders while pursuing the crusade planned by Innocent III. An experienced Roman administrator, he confirmed the Dominican order and approved the Franciscan Rule and encouraged clerical learning. His patient negotiations with Frederick II sought an expedition the emperor repeatedly delayed; the failure of the Fifth Crusade made that unfulfilled promise increasingly urgent.
people.biography:
Cencio had served as papal chamberlain and compiled the Liber censuum, recording the Roman Church’s revenues, possessions and obligations. Elected at Perugia in 1216, he brought this administrative experience to the task of implementing Lateran IV’s programme. His government relied on legates, finance and negotiations as much as broad declarations.

The Fifth Crusade captured Damietta in Egypt but ended in defeat amid divided leadership and difficult strategic decisions. Honorius continued pressing Frederick II to fulfil his crusading vow, accepting repeated postponements because he considered imperial participation essential. He crowned Frederick in 1220, although the emperor’s German and Sicilian power remained a danger to papal independence.

Honorius’s enduring religious legacy includes confirmation of the Dominican order in 1216 and approval of the Franciscan Rule in 1223. He supported the growing friars’ missions and protected their place within the Church. He also encouraged theological education and supported the young Henry III’s government in England after John’s death. Relations with Frederick were deteriorating when Honorius died in March 1227, before the open rupture under Gregory IX.

actions.text: Confirmed the Dominican order and approved the Franciscan Rule, giving stable canonical form to new communities of preaching and poverty.
Organized financing and diplomacy for the Fifth Crusade and continued negotiations over Frederick II’s crusading vow.
Supported education and compiled the Liber censuum, an important record of papal economic government.

people.context: Mendicant friars differed from monks enclosed in a single landed monastery: preaching, study and urban life were central to their mission. Honorius helped make these new institutions part of the Church’s structures. At the same time, his crusading policy showed the problem of depending on an emperor whose political consolidation the papacy also feared.

His patient negotiations with Frederick II sought an expedition the emperor repeatedly delayed; the failure of the Fifth Crusade made that unfulfilled promise increasingly urgent.

paragraphs.text: Cencio had served as papal chamberlain and compiled the Liber censuum, recording the Roman Church’s revenues, possessions and obligations. Elected at Perugia in 1216, he brought this administrative experience to the task of implementing Lateran IV’s programme. His government relied on legates, finance and negotiations as much as broad declarations.

The Fifth Crusade captured Damietta in Egypt but ended in defeat amid divided leadership and difficult strategic decisions. Honorius continued pressing Frederick II to fulfil his crusading vow, accepting repeated postponements because he considered imperial participation essential. He crowned Frederick in 1220, although the emperor’s German and Sicilian power remained a danger to papal independence.

Honorius’s enduring religious legacy includes confirmation of the Dominican order in 1216 and approval of the Franciscan Rule in 1223. He supported the growing friars’ missions and protected their place within the Church. He also encouraged theological education and supported the young Henry III’s government in England after John’s death. Relations with Frederick were deteriorating when Honorius died in March 1227, before the open rupture under Gregory IX.

actions.text: Confirmed the Dominican order and approved the Franciscan Rule, giving stable canonical form to new communities of preaching and poverty.
Organized financing and diplomacy for the Fifth Crusade and continued negotiations over Frederick II’s crusading vow.
Supported education and compiled the Liber censuum, an important record of papal economic government.

paragraphs.text: Mendicant friars differed from monks enclosed in a single landed monastery: preaching, study and urban life were central to their mission. Honorius helped make these new institutions part of the Church’s structures. At the same time, his crusading policy showed the problem of depending on an emperor whose political consolidation the papacy also feared.

people.summary: Gregory IX joined support for Francis and Dominic to powerful legal and coercive institutions. He commissioned the Decretals of 1234, a foundational collection of canon law, and appointed papal inquisitors against heresy. His struggle with Frederick II began over a delayed crusade and expanded into warfare over Italy, ending with the pope’s death while the emperor threatened Rome.
people.biography:
Ugolino of Ostia had long served as a diplomat and mediator before becoming pope in 1227. He knew Francis and Dominic, protected their communities and later canonized both founders. His support helped the new mendicant orders become central to preaching, missions and learning rather than marginal experiments.

When Frederick II returned from an attempted departure for the East in 1227, citing illness, Gregory treated the delay as another broken promise and excommunicated him. Frederick then went east while still under censure and negotiated a settlement concerning Jerusalem. In Italy, papal and imperial forces fought. Peace at San Germano in 1230 restored communion, but conflicts over Sicily, Lombardy and papal territory reopened the struggle in 1239.

Gregory commissioned Raymond of Peñafort’s collection of decretals, promulgated in 1234, organizing a vast body of papal law. He also appointed Dominican inquisitors, strengthening papal direction of investigations previously centred on bishops. Heresy convictions could lead to imprisonment or transfer for execution by secular authorities. Attempts to assemble a council in 1241 were obstructed by imperial capture of travelling prelates; Gregory died that August.

actions.text: Promulgated the Decretals of 1234, making papal case law a coherent foundation for legal study and church government.
Protected the mendicant orders and canonized Francis and Dominic.
Appointed papal inquisitors, expanding an institutional system that subjected dissenters to coercive investigation and severe punishment.
Excommunicated Frederick II and fought over imperial expansion in Italy; the conflict obstructed a general council.

people.context: The friars’ voluntary poverty and preaching offered a response to criticism of clerical wealth, but the same orders could be assigned inquisitorial functions. Gregory’s papacy therefore cannot be reduced either to spiritual renewal or political combat. Expanding legal administration made papal authority more effective, while the union of religious judgment and secular penalties made its treatment of dissent more coercive.

people.summary: Celestine IV was elected during a crisis of war and enforced confinement, then died after only weeks in office. Goffredo da Castiglione had served as a cardinal and legate, but left no developed papal programme. His election reveals how secular pressure could obstruct the cardinals’ freedom.
people.biography:
Goffredo came from the Milanese Castiglione family and served as chancellor in Milan before Gregory IX made him a cardinal. His northern Italian legations involved civic disputes, church property and opposition to heresy. Later claims that he was certainly Urban III’s nephew or a Cistercian monk lack adequate support.

After Gregory died in 1241, two cardinals remained imperial prisoners. Senator Matteo Rosso Orsini confined the other electors in the Septizonium to force a choice. Goffredo was elected in October and died in November. Accounts differ over whether he received consecration; no substantial programme of papal acts survives.

actions.text: Undertook northern Italian legations before his election; illness and death prevented sustained action as pope.

people.context: Imperial imprisonment and Roman confinement constrained the election from different sides. The episode preceded the formal conclave legislation of 1274 and was followed by a prolonged vacancy.

people.summary: Innocent IV was a canon lawyer whose contest with Frederick II reached the formal deposition of an emperor at Lyon. He governed from exile, supported missions beyond Europe and approved Clare of Assisi’s rule. His reign also authorized torture in heresy investigations through Ad extirpanda, an enduring and harmful expansion of coercive religious procedure.
people.biography:
Sinibaldo Fieschi came from Genoa and trained in law before serving as a cardinal and papal administrator. His election in 1243 ended the long vacancy after Celestine IV. Early negotiations with Frederick II failed over captured prelates, occupied territory and mutual distrust. Innocent escaped Italy with Genoese assistance and established himself at Lyon.

At the First Council of Lyon in 1245 he declared Frederick deposed and encouraged rival German kings. The struggle continued beyond the emperor’s death in 1250, as Innocent sought to prevent Frederick’s heirs from holding Sicily. He returned to Italy but suffered military reverses against Manfred shortly before dying in 1254. The political campaign placed heavy demands on papal finances and relations with other churches.

His wider government included missions toward the Mongols, support for eastern Christian contacts and approval of the Poor Clares’ rule in 1253. As a jurist he wrote an influential commentary on the decretals. In 1252 Ad extirpanda authorized the use of torture to obtain information in heresy cases, with stated limits against death or mutilation. Those limits did not remove the violence or unreliability of coerced confession, and subsequent practice exposed grave abuses.

actions.text: Deposed Frederick II at Lyon and pursued opposition to Hohenstaufen rule after the emperor’s death.
Supported missions and approved Clare’s rule, extending papal activity beyond the imperial struggle.
Authorized torture through Ad extirpanda, helping embed coercive interrogation in inquisitorial practice.
Produced an influential legal commentary that shaped later canon-law discussion.

people.context: Lyon offered relative safety for a pope unable to act freely in Italy. The council asserted spiritual authority over an emperor, but enforcing that judgment required money, armies and alternative rulers. Meanwhile the growing legal machinery of the Church reached further into ordinary lives; the authorization of torture extended that authority through physical coercion.

people.summary: Alexander IV protected the Franciscans and defended the friars’ place in university life, yet struggled politically against Manfred of Sicily. He continued the attempt to place an alternative dynasty in the southern kingdom, drawing England into an expensive project that never succeeded. His reign shows the widening gap between papal spiritual influence and the resources needed to enforce temporal claims.
people.biography:
Rinaldo of Segni had served as cardinal bishop of Ostia and protector of the Franciscans before succeeding Innocent IV in 1254. He continued that concern as pope, canonizing Clare of Assisi and supporting the friars during the controversy led by William of Saint-Amour at Paris. The dispute concerned whether mendicants should teach, preach and hear confessions alongside existing clergy.

In southern Italy Alexander renewed opposition to Manfred and in 1255 confirmed his predecessor’s grant of the Sicilian crown to Edmund, son of Henry III of England. The arrangement depended on money and military intervention that the English king could not provide. Papal demands associated with the project deepened resentment among English clergy and political society.

Manfred consolidated his rule, and the Ghibelline victory at Montaperti in 1260 weakened the pope’s allies in central Italy. Alexander also had difficulty governing Rome and resided at Viterbo, where he died in 1261. His support for religious renewal proved more durable than his attempts to direct the Italian balance of power.

actions.text: Protected the friars in the Paris university dispute and canonized Clare of Assisi.
Confirmed Innocent IV’s grant of Sicily to Edmund of England, seeking an alternative to Manfred but generating heavy financial controversy.
Opposed Ghibelline expansion in Italy while unable to secure a decisive military settlement.

people.context: Mendicant communities challenged older arrangements because their members taught and ministered without depending on the same local structures as secular masters and parish clergy. Meanwhile the Sicilian project made the Church’s international finances serve a contested dynastic policy. These two conflicts explain why Alexander could be influential in religious institutions and politically vulnerable at the same time.

people.summary: Urban IV is remembered liturgically for establishing Corpus Christi and politically for inviting Charles of Anjou into the struggle for Sicily. Born Jacques Pantaléon, he rose from a tradesman’s family to become patriarch of Jerusalem and then pope. His short reign reorganized papal finances and alliances, preparing changes in Italian politics that he did not live to see.
people.biography:
Jacques served at Laon and Liège before diplomatic missions in northern Europe, the bishopric of Verdun and the patriarchate of Jerusalem. He was at Viterbo when the cardinals elected him in 1261, although he was not one of their number. His experience combined knowledge of European courts with the precarious situation of eastern Christians.

Urban judged that papal forces could not dislodge Manfred from Sicily without an outside ruler. He reorganized finances, strengthened the Guelf party and negotiated with Charles of Anjou, brother of Louis IX. The proposed settlement required Sicily to remain separate from the empire and bound its king to papal obligations. Creating new cardinals also shifted the balance within the college toward France.

His earlier experience at Liège connected him with the movement for a Eucharistic feast promoted by Juliana of Cornillon. In 1264 he instituted Corpus Christi for the universal Church and commissioned Thomas Aquinas’s liturgical texts. Reception spread more gradually after his death. Urban died at Perugia in 1264 before Charles’s conquest of the southern kingdom.

actions.text: Negotiated the Angevin intervention in Sicily, changing the direction of Italian dynastic politics.
Reorganized papal finance and enlarged the cardinalate to support his programme.
Instituted Corpus Christi and commissioned its liturgical office, linking a local devotional movement with universal worship.

people.context: The restoration of Byzantine rule at Constantinople in 1261 altered eastern diplomacy, while Manfred’s power threatened the papacy in Italy. Urban dealt with these overlapping interests pragmatically, using finance, cardinals and foreign alliances. His Eucharistic initiative also shows how a movement supported by women religious and local clergy could eventually reshape the wider Church’s calendar.

people.summary: Clement IV carried through the alliance that brought Charles of Anjou to the Sicilian throne. Before becoming a churchman, Gui Foucois had been married, a father and a prominent legal adviser. As pope he financed a war preached as a crusade, then faced the harsh rule of the victorious ally whose power was supposed to protect papal independence.
people.biography:
Gui came from Saint-Gilles and pursued a legal and royal-service career after a period of military life. After his wife died, he entered the clergy, becoming bishop of Le Puy, archbishop of Narbonne and cardinal bishop of Sabina. He was chosen pope in 1265 after a vacancy dominated by debate over the Italian crisis.

Clement supported Charles of Anjou with legates, preaching and difficult financial arrangements. Charles’s victory over Manfred at Benevento in 1266 established Angevin rule in the south. Clement repeatedly reminded the new king of his obligations and criticized abuses by royal officials, but remained committed to him when Conradin attempted to recover the Hohenstaufen inheritance.

Conradin’s defeat at Tagliacozzo in 1268 was followed by his execution at Naples. The later story that Clement advised the killing lacks reliable support; he protested Charles’s cruelty. The pope nevertheless bore responsibility for supporting the political alliance that enabled the conquest. He died at Viterbo in November 1268, and the cardinals then took nearly three years to choose a successor.

actions.text: Completed the Angevin alliance and helped finance Charles’s conquest of Sicily.
Rebuked the victorious king’s abuses while continuing to support his dynasty.
Restricted relatives’ opportunities to profit from his election.

people.context: The use of crusading privileges against an Italian dynastic opponent blurred the boundary between defence of the faith and papal territorial policy. Replacing Hohenstaufen power did not remove the problem of a dominant southern king. Clement’s negotiations and admonitions show the difficulty of controlling an ally after military victory had made that ally indispensable.

people.summary: Gregory X tried to turn a crisis in papal government into institutional reform. Elected after nearly three years of deadlock while he was in the Holy Land, he convened the Second Council of Lyon and established strict enclosure rules for future elections. He also sought peace among rulers, a new crusade and reconciliation with the Byzantine Church.
people.biography:
Teobaldo Visconti of Piacenza had served churchmen and travelled widely before becoming archdeacon of Liège. He was at Acre with Prince Edward of England when a delegated group of cardinals finally elected him in 1271. He returned to Italy, accepted the office and received ordination and consecration in 1272.

The Second Council of Lyon in 1274 brought together his principal aims. It approved financial preparations for a crusade, addressed church discipline and received a Byzantine delegation professing union with Rome. The agreement had limited support among Greek Christians and did not become a lasting reconciliation. Gregory also recognized Rudolf of Habsburg, seeking an end to the prolonged German royal uncertainty.

The election that had brought Gregory to office shaped Ubi periculum: cardinals were to remain enclosed, with restricted provisions if they delayed choosing a pope. This made the conclave a legal institution rather than leaving enclosure to angry local authorities. Gregory died at Arezzo in January 1276. His immediate successors did not all preserve the rule, but it later became foundational.

people.summary: Innocent V was the first Dominican pope, bringing the experience of a Paris theologian to a reign of only five months. Formerly Peter of Tarentaise, he had helped shape the Second Council of Lyon. As pope he pursued peace among Italian factions and rulers and tried to sustain the council’s fragile agreement with the Greek Church.
people.biography:
Peter came from Tarentaise and joined the Dominicans as a young man. He became a master of theology at Paris and a prominent teacher, then served as a provincial superior, archbishop of Lyon and cardinal bishop of Ostia. At the council of 1274 he spoke to the assembled fathers and delivered Bonaventure’s funeral address.

Chosen after Gregory X’s death in January 1276, Innocent inherited an ambitious programme: a crusade, reconciliation among rulers and implementation of the Greek union. He mediated between Rudolf of Habsburg and Charles of Anjou and sought peace among Italian cities, including Pisa and Lucca. His early death in June prevented these initiatives from becoming a sustained policy.

His intellectual legacy was more extensive than his papal legislation. A commentary on Peter Lombard’s Sentences and other theological writings linked him to the school culture in which Dominican thinkers combined teaching, disputation and service to the wider Church. His later recognition as Blessed is affirmed by the official Vatican saint listing.

people.summary: Adrian V’s papacy lasted only a few weeks, so his major achievements belong to his earlier diplomatic career. As Ottobono Fieschi he helped reconcile Henry III’s government and defeated English barons. Elected amid Angevin influence in 1276, he suspended Gregory X’s strict conclave rules but died before replacing them with a new system.
people.biography:
Ottobono belonged to the Genoese Fieschi family and was a nephew of Innocent IV. His long cardinalate involved curial diplomacy and support for Angevin policy in Italy. As papal legate in England after the Battle of Evesham, he supported the king while seeking restraint toward defeated opponents and a settlement that could end continuing conflict.

His mediation contributed to the reconciliation associated with the Dictum of Kenilworth. The mission shows a diplomat working beyond the simple division of royal supporters and rebels: peace required terms under which the defeated could recover a place in political society.

After Innocent V’s death, Ottobono became Adrian V in July 1276. He suspended the electoral enclosure legislation introduced at Lyon, intending revision. Death at Viterbo the following month prevented that work. John XXI later issued the formal suspension, and long vacancies returned.

actions.text: Mediated in England after the Barons’ War, helping bring defeated parties toward settlement.
Suspended strict conclave rules with a view to revision, but died before producing replacements.

people.context: Gregory X’s rules sought to prevent deadlock, but enclosure could also expose electors to pressure from the ruler controlling the city. Charles of Anjou’s influence during the 1276 election helps explain why electoral speed and electoral freedom could appear to be competing concerns.

people.summary: John XXI was the Portuguese pope whose brief reign combined diplomacy, church-union negotiations and revision of electoral rules. Traditionally celebrated as the physician and author Peter of Spain, his precise relationship to works carrying that name remains debated. He died from injuries when part of the papal palace at Viterbo collapsed, leaving another unfinished programme.
people.biography:
Peter Julian’s Portuguese ecclesiastical career is better documented than the early academic biography traditionally attached to him. Several writers and physicians were called Peter of Spain, leaving the authorship of famous medical and logical works associated with that name disputed. He became archbishop-elect of Braga and cardinal bishop of Tusculum before his election in 1276.

As pope he confirmed the suspension of Gregory X’s conclave rules and planned revised procedures. He sought to restrain Charles of Anjou’s dominance in Italy while negotiating with Rudolf of Habsburg. Legates also worked to prevent war between France and Castile, important if the western rulers were to cooperate in a new crusade.

John sent envoys to Constantinople to implement the union negotiated at Lyon. He also requested inquiry into reports of erroneous teaching at Paris; that request was distinct from the local bishop’s condemnation of propositions in 1277. In May part of his Viterbo residence collapsed, and he died of his injuries. Rumours of magic belong to hostile later stories, not a sound explanation of the accident.

Mediated among western rulers and continued negotiations with the Byzantine Church.
Requested investigation of disputed teaching at Paris amid intense debate over philosophy and theology.

people.context: Theologians and masters of arts were debating the implications of newly available Aristotelian learning. John’s reputation as a learned pope belongs within that culture, although the shared name Peter of Spain leaves the authorship of several surviving treatises uncertain. His political task likewise required balancing several rulers and Angevin ambitions.

people.summary: Nicholas III sought to free the papacy from excessive dependence on Charles of Anjou and consolidate its government in central Italy. A Roman Orsini cardinal with decades of curial experience, he also issued an influential interpretation of Franciscan poverty and enlarged the Vatican residence. His programme strengthened papal institutions but distributed important offices and territories to relatives.
people.biography:
Giovanni Gaetano Orsini had served since Innocent IV’s time and acquired influence in elections, diplomacy and Franciscan affairs. Elected in 1277 after another long vacancy, he brought a Roman noble family’s networks to the task of government. Those connections gave him resources but also encouraged the nepotism for which his memory became notorious.

Nicholas obtained Rudolf of Habsburg’s renunciation of claims in Romagna and required Charles of Anjou to give up the Roman senatorship and Tuscan regency. Reserving Roman municipal offices to citizens limited the direct hold of foreign monarchs. Yet he placed relatives in influential positions, including administration of newly secured territory.

In 1279 Exiit qui seminat interpreted the Franciscan rule and supported a strict account of the friars’ poverty. He continued efforts to implement the Lyon union with the Greeks while restraining Angevin ambitions in the East. At the Vatican he remodelled the palace and acquired adjacent land, helping establish the residence and gardens. He died in 1280 before many of his diplomatic plans matured.

actions.text: Secured Romagna for papal government and reduced Charles of Anjou’s direct authority in Rome and Tuscany.
Issued Exiit qui seminat, a major interpretation of Franciscan poverty.
Expanded the Vatican residence while advancing relatives into powerful offices.

people.context: The papacy needed protection from foreign domination, but the practical alternative could be government through a pope’s own family. Nicholas’s reign exposes that tension. The Franciscan poverty debate also raised a difficult institutional question: how could a growing order use buildings and goods while claiming the radical poverty of its founder?

people.summary: Martin IV reversed Nicholas III’s restraint of Angevin power and tied papal policy closely to Charles of Anjou. His rupture with Michael VIII undermined the Lyon union, while the Sicilian Vespers transformed the struggle for the island into a wider war. He used censures and crusading privileges against Peter III of Aragon, but could not restore Charles’s control of Sicily.
people.biography:
Simon de Brion served the French monarchy and became a cardinal and papal legate. His work in France included reform synods and support for the Angevin enterprise. At the election of 1281, Charles’s supporters detained influential Italian cardinals, helping secure a result favourable to a French candidate. Martin was crowned at Orvieto and never established a stable residence in Rome.

He restored Charles to the Roman senatorship and supported plans against Byzantine Constantinople. Excommunicating Michael VIII moved the papacy away from the policy of church union pursued since Gregory X. Religious censures thus became entangled with Charles’s projected eastern conquests.

The Sicilian Vespers of 1282 began a violent rejection of Angevin rule. The Sicilians accepted Peter III of Aragon, and Martin responded by excommunicating him, declaring his Aragonese throne forfeit and supporting a crusade. The effort failed to recover Sicily for the Angevins. Martin died at Perugia in 1285, leaving his successors a conflict that could no longer be solved by a simple demand for obedience.

Excommunicated Michael VIII, undermining the diplomatic basis of the Lyon church union.
Supported a crusade against Peter III after the Sicilian revolt, extending the dynastic conflict to Aragon.

people.context: Sicilian resistance arose from the realities of Angevin rule, while Aragon had dynastic and strategic reasons to intervene. Treating every opponent as merely a disobedient papal vassal missed the strength of those interests. Martin’s policies show how dependence on one king could narrow papal diplomacy and damage relations with other Christian churches.

people.summary: Honorius IV tried to moderate the consequences of Martin IV’s policies without abandoning Angevin claims to Sicily. A Roman nobleman severely affected by gout, he governed during a relatively peaceful period in the Papal States. His legislation sought protection for Sicilian subjects against royal abuse, while diplomacy aimed at a settlement that his short reign could not complete.
people.biography:
Giacomo Savelli had been a cardinal for decades and participated in important elections and diplomatic negotiations. The cardinals elected him rapidly in 1285, partly to avoid renewed outside interference. He was physically disabled by gout and needed assistance even in celebrating Mass, but remained actively involved in government.

Honorius maintained the papal and Angevin claims to Sicily and continued to reject the Aragonese rulers. At the same time, his constitution of 1285 prescribed protections against abuses by the king and officials and allowed appeals to Rome. This was an attempt to reform the government whose restoration he supported, rather than simply overlook the grievances behind the revolt.

He resumed negotiations with Rudolf of Habsburg and participated in efforts, encouraged by Edward I, to reduce conflict in the western Mediterranean. Rome and papal territories enjoyed greater stability than under his predecessor. He also supported religious orders and advocated study of eastern languages for missionaries. He died in 1287 before the Sicilian negotiations reached a lasting settlement.

actions.text: Issued ordinances intended to protect Sicilian subjects against royal and official abuses.
Maintained Angevin claims while pursuing negotiations with Aragon and the German king.
Supported religious communities and study of eastern languages for missionary work.

people.context: The conflict after the Vespers involved rival dynasties, the papacy’s overlordship claims and the population’s experience of rule. Honorius recognized the need for just administration but could not resolve the contradiction between that recognition and insistence on restoring an unwanted dynasty. His relatively stable Roman government gave him more room for diplomacy than several predecessors had enjoyed.

people.summary: Nicholas IV was the first Franciscan pope, a former minister general with experience of negotiations with the Greeks. He supported missions reaching toward Asia and confronted the loss of Acre in 1291. In Italy his reliance on the Colonna family and continued support for Angevin claims to Sicily complicated efforts to secure peace and independent papal government.
people.biography:
Girolamo Masci entered the Franciscans from a modest background and became a delegate to Constantinople before the Second Council of Lyon. He succeeded Bonaventure as minister general and later became a cardinal. His election in 1288 followed a long vacancy interrupted by disease and the departure of most electors from Rome.

As pope he continued to support the Angevin dynasty, crowning Charles II at Rieti and rejecting a settlement that would have recognized Aragonese possession of Sicily. The policy failed to end the war. At Rome the Colonna exercised conspicuous influence, showing that a friar pope still depended on powerful aristocratic networks for practical government.

The fall of Acre in 1291 ended the principal mainland crusader foothold in the Holy Land. Nicholas appealed for a new expedition and discussion of cooperation between military orders, but achieved no lasting military recovery. His mission policy had wider consequences: he sent John of Montecorvino toward Asia and supported contacts with other eastern peoples. He also granted the cardinals a share of papal revenues and administration. He died in 1292, followed by another prolonged vacancy.

Within Italy, the pope’s spiritual background did not remove the need for family alliances or solve the dynastic conflict over Sicily.

people.summary: Celestine V was an elderly hermit chosen to end more than two years of electoral deadlock. His life of prayer inspired hopes for a renewed Church, but the demands of government and the influence of Charles II of Naples overwhelmed his brief reign. He freely resigned in 1294, a decisive precedent showing that papal office could be relinquished.
people.biography:
Peter of Morrone pursued solitary prayer in the Abruzzi, but followers gathered around him and developed a Benedictine congregation. His spiritual reputation reached far beyond the hermitage. When the cardinals remained divided after Nicholas IV’s death, they turned to this figure outside their political contest and elected him in July 1294.

Crowned at L’Aquila, Peter took the name Celestine V and granted the Perdonanza, a special indulgence emphasizing reconciliation and mercy. Yet his court moved to Naples under Charles II’s influence, and appointments and privileges proved difficult to administer. He also restored Gregory X’s strict electoral rules, an institutional act with a much longer life than his own administration.

After consulting on whether a pope could resign, Celestine declared that such resignation was possible and stepped down in December. His successor Boniface VIII feared that opponents would use the former pope as a rival focus of obedience. After attempted escape, Peter was confined at Fumone and died in 1296. His detention was real; stories of a proven murder are not established by the consulted evidence. Clement V canonized him in 1313.

actions.text: Founded a community rooted in eremitical Benedictine life.
Granted the Perdonanza indulgence, expressing a lasting pastoral concern for forgiveness.
Restored conclave rules and established a clear legal precedent for voluntary papal resignation.

people.context: Reform hopes often imagined that a holy outsider could cleanse institutions corrupted by power. Celestine’s election tested that hope against a curia requiring legal expertise, administrative coordination and political independence. His resignation ended his exercise of temporal government without ending his reputation for holiness.

people.summary: Boniface VIII combined a lawyer’s vision of papal authority with a forceful and often divisive political style. He proclaimed the first Jubilee in 1300 and strengthened canon-law institutions, but his clash with Philip IV of France exposed the limits of medieval papal power. Captured at Anagni in 1303, he died soon after his release, leaving a conflict that shaped the next generation.
people.biography:
Benedetto Caetani had served as a lawyer, diplomat and cardinal before succeeding the resigned Celestine V in 1294. He defended the validity of that resignation and his own election, while keeping the former pope under confinement lest opponents use him as an alternative claimant. Rivalry with the Colonna family escalated into deprivation of its cardinals, a military campaign and destruction of its stronghold at Palestrina.

War between England and France brought the taxation of clergy into dispute. Clericis laicos restricted such taxation without papal permission; royal retaliation then forced practical concessions. A renewed crisis over the prosecution of Bishop Bernard Saisset led Boniface to assert the spiritual authority of the papacy more sharply. Unam sanctam in 1302 expressed the unity of the Church and the superior end served by spiritual power, in terms that intensified the political conflict.

Boniface’s 1300 Jubilee drew pilgrims to Rome and established a recurring institution of penitence and pardon. His government also produced the Liber Sextus collection of canon law and supported learning, including the Roman studium. These achievements mattered beyond the struggle with kings.

Philip’s agents and Sciarra Colonna seized Boniface at Anagni in September 1303, intending to force submission or removal. Townspeople freed him after several days, but he died in Rome the next month. The armed detention is well attested, while the famous physical slap and other polemical stories remain uncertain. The episode exposed how vulnerable a pope could be to organized royal force.

actions.text: Proclaimed the first Jubilee and fostered Rome’s role as a destination for penitential pilgrimage.
Promulgated the Liber Sextus, continuing the systematization of canon law.
Defended clerical jurisdiction and papal authority against Philip IV, culminating in Unam sanctam.
Used military force against the Colonna, a decision that deepened the hostility surrounding his final crisis.

people.context: Royal governments increasingly raised taxes, used trained lawyers and claimed authority over subjects within their territories. Boniface’s universal conception of papal responsibility met these stronger monarchies and their propaganda campaigns. His own family politics and coercive methods also created enemies at home, allowing royal and aristocratic opposition to combine at Anagni.

people.summary: Benedict XI tried to restore peace after Boniface VIII’s humiliation without declaring the attack on his predecessor acceptable. A Dominican teacher and former master general, he had remained loyal during the crisis at Anagni. His eight-month papacy eased relations with Philip IV and the Colonna while maintaining censures against principal participants in the assault.
people.biography:
Nicholas Boccasini entered the Dominicans as a young man, studied and taught theology, and became master general in 1296. He defended Boniface VIII’s legitimacy and participated in diplomatic efforts to reconcile Edward I and Philip IV. Later a cardinal and bishop of Ostia, he also served as legate in Hungary.

After the seizure of Boniface at Anagni, Nicholas’s loyalty helped make him an acceptable successor. Elected in October 1303, he chose a conciliatory policy toward France. He removed censures and restored privileges while seeking to prevent the quarrel from becoming a permanent breach between the French crown and the Holy See.

His clemency had limits: Guillaume de Nogaret, Sciarra Colonna and others implicated in the attack remained subject to proceedings. The Colonna cardinals were absolved but were not simply returned to their former positions. Benedict died at Perugia in July 1304 before the settlement was secure. Poisoning rumours are not established evidence. The Church remembers him as Blessed, with a reputation for peace and gentleness.

actions.text: Sought reconciliation with Philip IV after the confrontation inherited from Boniface VIII.
Distinguished broader reconciliation from accountability for the principal attackers at Anagni.
Brought long Dominican experience in teaching, leadership and mediation to a short papacy.

people.context: The pope had to preserve the authority of his office while avoiding another confrontation with a powerful monarchy. His decisions show that forgiveness and institutional defence were not necessarily identical to abandoning a predecessor. His sudden death again left the cardinals divided, and the next pope would establish the court at Avignon.

people.summary: Clement V began the long period in which the popes governed from Avignon. A Gascon archbishop elected after a divided conclave, he faced intense pressure from Philip IV of France over Boniface VIII’s memory and the Templars. At Vienne he suppressed the Templar order without a definitive judicial conviction of the order as a whole, a distinction essential to understanding its destruction.
people.biography:
Bertrand de Got had served as bishop of Comminges and archbishop of Bordeaux before his election in 1305. He was crowned at Lyon and remained in southern France rather than travelling to Rome. Italian insecurity, the court’s networks and the demands of negotiation encouraged the move to Avignon in 1309. The city was then outside the French royal domain, although French influence over papal affairs was considerable.

Philip IV pressed for condemnation of Boniface VIII and acted against the Templars in 1307 without waiting for ordinary papal process. Clement protested the seizure of authority, but then ordered wider investigation. Tortured confessions, retractions and executions severely compromised the possibility of a fair defence. The distinction between the guilt of individuals and the status of the order became central.

At the Council of Vienne, Clement suppressed the order in 1312 by papal provision rather than a definitive judgment proving the order collectively heretical. He assigned its property to the Hospitallers, though royal control and costs complicated the transfer. He also negotiated around Henry VII’s imperial expedition and prepared the Clementines, a collection of canon law formally republished under John XXII. He died in 1314.

actions.text: Established the papal court at Avignon, beginning a durable change in the geography of church government.
Summoned Vienne and suppressed the Templars amid royal pressure and a deeply compromised process.

Military orders faced criticism after the loss of the Holy Land, and their wealth attracted rulers, but those conditions do not prove the charges used against them. Papally ordered inquiry and juridical proceedings were constrained by the power of a king who controlled the prisoners.

people.summary: John XXII made Avignon a more permanent centre of papal administration. His energetic government expanded appointments and finance, but also provoked resistance. Disputes with the Franciscans over poverty and with Louis of Bavaria over imperial authority became intertwined. Near the end of his life, his sermons on the beatific vision caused a theological controversy that his successor had to resolve.
people.biography:
Jacques Duèze, a lawyer and church administrator from Cahors, became pope in 1316 after another long vacancy. He settled at Avignon and directed a large correspondence across Europe and beyond. Publishing the Clementines and organizing the curia strengthened the legal apparatus of government; reserving appointments and collecting associated revenues also sharpened criticism of papal centralization.

John rejected claims that Christ and the apostles possessed nothing either individually or in common, and resisted Franciscan arguments that earlier papal arrangements about poverty bound all successors. The conflict drove Michael of Cesena, William of Ockham and others toward the protection of Louis of Bavaria. Some dissenting friars faced heresy proceedings and execution. John’s confrontation with Louis likewise concerned whether a German ruler could exercise imperial authority without papal approval.

Louis supported Nicholas V as a rival pope in 1328, but the claimant’s position collapsed and he submitted at Avignon in 1330. John’s own sermons then questioned whether the blessed saw God before the final resurrection. Theologians opposed him, and John clarified that he had offered an opinion rather than a definitive judgment. He withdrew the position before dying in 1334. Benedict XII would issue the authoritative definition.

actions.text: Expanded curial government and promulgated the Clementines, while increasing reliance on papal appointments and revenues.
Challenged Franciscan theories of absolute poverty, leading to a serious rupture within the order.
Opposed Louis of Bavaria and received the submission of the rival Nicholas V.
Provoked debate on the beatific vision through nondefinitive sermons, and withdrew his disputed position before death.

people.context: A question about evangelical poverty became a question about the limits of papal authority: could a pope reverse a predecessor’s arrangements, and could critics appeal beyond him? Louis’s conflict with the papacy gave dissident thinkers political shelter. The beatific-vision debate also illustrates the distinction between a pope’s personal theological argument and a formal teaching intended to settle doctrine.

paragraphs.text: Jacques Duèze, a lawyer and church administrator from Cahors, became pope in 1316 after another long vacancy. He settled at Avignon and directed a large correspondence across Europe and beyond. Publishing the Clementines and organizing the curia strengthened the legal apparatus of government; reserving appointments and collecting associated revenues also sharpened criticism of papal centralization.

John rejected claims that Christ and the apostles possessed nothing either individually or in common, and resisted Franciscan arguments that earlier papal arrangements about poverty bound all successors. The conflict drove Michael of Cesena, William of Ockham and others toward the protection of Louis of Bavaria. Some dissenting friars faced heresy proceedings and execution. John’s confrontation with Louis likewise concerned whether a German ruler could exercise imperial authority without papal approval.

Louis supported Nicholas V as a rival pope in 1328, but the claimant’s position collapsed and he submitted at Avignon in 1330. John’s own sermons then questioned whether the blessed saw God before the final resurrection. Theologians opposed him, and John clarified that he had offered an opinion rather than a definitive judgment. He withdrew the position before dying in 1334. Benedict XII would issue the authoritative definition.

Louis’s conflict with the papacy gave dissident thinkers political shelter. The beatific-vision debate also illustrates the distinction between a pope’s personal theological argument and a formal teaching intended to settle doctrine.

people.summary: Benedict XII was a Cistercian theologian who pursued administrative and monastic reform while maintaining the papacy at Avignon. His constitution Benedictus Deus settled the controversy over the blessed seeing God before the Last Judgment. His earlier career as an inquisitorial bishop also left unusually detailed records of ordinary lives, produced within a coercive system of investigation and punishment.
people.biography:
Jacques Fournier rose through Cistercian education and the abbacy of Fontfroide to become bishop of Pamiers. There he personally investigated suspected heresy. The surviving records preserve extensive testimony from his diocese, including the pressures placed on those interrogated and the punishments imposed. He later became cardinal and a leading theological adviser before election in 1334.

Benedict ordered clergy without duties at Avignon to return to their churches, sought limits on excessive appointments and fees, and opposed the enrichment of relatives. He issued detailed reforms for monastic communities, linking discipline, regular chapters, administration and study. These measures sought to make an increasingly centralized Church function more honestly rather than dismantle centralization itself.

After consultation and study, Benedictus Deus in 1336 defined that souls needing no further purification enjoy the direct vision of God before the resurrection and general judgment. Benedict also developed the fortified papal residence at Avignon. Plans for return to Italy and reconciliation with Louis of Bavaria failed amid political opposition. He died in 1342, with the court more firmly established on the Rhône.

Developed Avignon’s papal palace while continuing to support Roman churches from afar.

people.context: The office had become dependent on a large apparatus of petitions, appointments and revenue. Benedict tried to discipline that apparatus, but Italian insecurity and French political interests complicated any return to Rome. His background also shows the close connection between theological expertise, pastoral authority and the investigation of dissent in the medieval Church.

people.summary: Clement VI presided over an Avignon court noted for splendour, artistic patronage and strong French connections. He purchased the city for the papacy and authorized the Jubilee of 1350 while remaining outside Rome. During the Black Death he issued protections for Jews accused of causing the plague, a notable intervention against persecution within an otherwise costly and nepotistic reign.
people.biography:
Pierre Roger entered the Benedictines as a child, studied and taught at Paris, and rose through important French bishoprics and royal service. He became pope in 1342. His court’s magnificence and generous patronage contrasted with Benedict XII’s austerity, and the promotion of relatives and Frenchmen increased criticism of the papacy’s partiality.

Clement pursued the conflict with Louis of Bavaria and supported Charles of Luxembourg’s election as German king. In 1348 he bought Avignon from Joanna of Naples, giving the papacy direct possession of the city where it already resided. He shortened the Jubilee interval to fifty years and permitted the 1350 celebration at Rome, but declined appeals to return there himself.

The plague reached Avignon in 1348. As Jews were blamed and attacked in many regions, Clement issued bulls defending them and offered refuge within papal territory. His diplomatic efforts in the Hundred Years War achieved only temporary truces. Court expenses and political commitments encouraged new fiscal demands and reservations of offices, drawing resistance such as England’s Statute of Provisors. He died in 1352.

Protected Jews against plague accusations and violence during the Black Death.
Supported Charles of Luxembourg against Louis of Bavaria while seeking truces between England and France.
Patronized art and learning, but financed an expensive court and advanced many relatives.

people.context: The Black Death was both a mortality catastrophe and a crisis of explanation, in which vulnerable minorities became targets. Clement’s intervention mattered because religious authority could either intensify or resist such persecution. Meanwhile the Hundred Years War made claims of impartial mediation difficult for a court whose personnel and interests appeared closely tied to France.

people.summary: Innocent VI sought a more restrained Avignon government and recovered papal authority in Italy through Cardinal Gil de Albornoz. A former law teacher and judge, he rejected electoral promises that would have divided papal power with the cardinals. His diplomacy helped the negotiations ending in Brétigny, but bands of unemployed soldiers still threatened Avignon and exposed the limits of ecclesiastical censures.
people.biography:
Étienne Aubert’s career began in civil law at Toulouse before bishoprics and senior curial offices. Elected in 1352, he had accepted an electoral agreement only insofar as it accorded with church law. Once pope, he declared the restrictions on papal authority invalid, a decision that became part of the long debate over whether cardinals could bind the man they elected.

He reduced courtly luxury, ordered clergy to reside in their benefices and assigned fixed incomes to judicial auditors to support more impartial administration. In Italy he commissioned Albornoz, whose military campaigns and diplomacy re-established papal rule over territories controlled by local lords. That recovery helped make a later papal return to Rome possible.

Innocent allowed Charles IV’s imperial coronation by a legate but required the emperor to leave Rome promptly. He also sought peace between England and France, and papal mediation contributed to the settlement at Brétigny in 1360. Free Companies of soldiers nevertheless ravaged France and threatened Avignon; fortifications and payments were required when censures failed. He died in 1362 before the court could return to Italy.

actions.text: Reduced curial luxury and promoted clerical residence and more regular judicial remuneration.
Entrusted Albornoz with restoring papal territorial government in Italy.
Supported negotiations leading toward Brétigny and fortified Avignon against mercenary companies.

people.context: The Hundred Years War produced mobile armed companies whose livelihoods depended on continued violence even during truces. They endangered the papal court as well as ordinary communities. In Italy, restoring government required accommodation with cities and lords alongside military force, showing why the pope’s geographical return depended on institutions and security rather than desire alone.

people.summary: Urban V attempted what earlier Avignon popes had postponed: returning the papal court to Rome. A Benedictine monk and canon lawyer, he entered the city in 1367 and restored churches and institutions, but political instability drew him back to Avignon in 1370. His support for universities and poor students, and his efforts to restrain patronage, formed another important part of his reforming programme.
people.biography:
Guillaume Grimoard studied law and theology, served as a teacher and Benedictine abbot, and undertook diplomatic missions in Italy. He was not a cardinal when elected in 1362. His monastic habits and legal expertise shaped a government concerned with discipline, education and practical administration.

Urban struggled against mercenary companies and the Visconti’s expansion while negotiating with French and Italian powers. Albornoz’s recovery of papal territory made a return possible. Despite resistance from French cardinals, Urban left Avignon in 1367 and entered Rome that October. He repaired basilicas and residences, supported work and food relief, and sought to restore the city’s religious life.

Charles IV visited, and the Byzantine emperor John V came seeking aid against Turkish expansion and personally professed communion with Rome. These ceremonies did not secure lasting political support. Albornoz’s death, Italian revolts and renewed Anglo-French warfare weakened Urban’s position. He returned to Avignon in 1370 despite appeals to remain, and died there in December. Pius IX approved his cult in 1870. Universities, student aid and educational foundations remained a durable legacy.

actions.text: Returned the papal court to Rome in 1367 and restored religious buildings and civic assistance.
Supported universities and the education of students without sufficient resources.
Pursued peace and eastern Christian contacts while struggling against mercenary violence.
Returned to Avignon in 1370 when the Italian position remained insecure.

people.context: A physical return could symbolize the Church’s attachment to Rome, but the Papal States still required dependable government and protection. France’s war, the interests of the cardinals and the ambitions of Italian rulers pulled the pope in different directions. Urban’s eventual withdrawal therefore explains why the permanent restoration under Gregory XI required another effort rather than following automatically from 1367.

people.summary: Gregory XI brought the papal court back from Avignon to Rome in 1377. His return, encouraged by Catherine of Siena, did not settle the wars and resentments surrounding papal government in Italy. Florence’s revolt and brutal warfare shadowed the move; the Western Schism began after his death.
people.biography:
Pierre Roger grew up within the powerful family of Clement VI. Ecclesiastical benefices and an exceptionally early cardinalate financed his education; legal study at Perugia helped form a pope accustomed to canonists, petitions and dynastic negotiation. His election at Avignon continued a French-dominated curial world, even as governing the Church required a renewed presence in Italy.

The conflict with Bernabò Visconti and Florence made that return hazardous. Gregory imposed an interdict on Florence and employed military force while Catherine sought reconciliation. He entered Rome in January 1377, but violence at Cesena under Cardinal Robert of Geneva intensified hostility. Disturbances drove him temporarily to Anagni. The move ended the Avignon residence without repairing the political relationships that would fracture in 1378.

actions.text: Returned the papal court to Rome, restoring its residence near the apostolic shrines after decades at Avignon.
Condemned propositions associated with John Wyclif in 1377, extending his government into disputes over doctrine and ecclesiastical authority.

people.context: Gregory’s diplomacy extended beyond the French–Italian problem. In southern Italy he mediated between the Angevin court of Joanna of Naples and the rulers of Sicily, combining marriage negotiations, feudal obligations and ecclesiastical privileges. Emperor Charles IV supported him against the Visconti, yet German clergy resisted papal taxation. These pressures explain why returning to Rome was more than a spiritual gesture: the papacy also had to sustain revenue, govern territories and negotiate with rulers whose interests differed sharply.

people.summary: Urban VI’s election in Rome was followed within months by a rival election and the Western Schism. A skilled administrator before becoming pope, he pursued reform with a confrontational style that alienated cardinals. His struggle with the Avignon obedience became entangled with the succession to Naples and violence against his own opponents.
people.biography:
Bartolomeo Prignano studied canon law, served in the Neapolitan Church and became an experienced official of the Avignon chancery. His reputation for ability and personal rigor made him an attractive candidate outside the College of Cardinals. The first conclave held in Rome after the return from Avignon took place amid intense popular demands for a Roman or Italian pope.

Cardinals initially recognized him, then challenged the election’s freedom and chose Robert of Geneva as Clement VII at Fondi. Urban maintained his own legitimacy. Later he replaced Joanna of Naples with Charles of Durazzo, but their alliance collapsed. During the ensuing struggle he imprisoned cardinals accused of plotting against him; torture and killings gravely damaged his government. His pontificate ended without reconciliation.

actions.text: Created new cardinals to sustain the Roman obedience after the rival election, institutionalizing a divided Church.
Planned a jubilee for 1390; the celebration would take place under his successor.

people.context: The dispute was not simply a quarrel between two personalities. Legal testimony about the conclave, the cardinals’ conception of their own authority, Roman civic pressure and princely alliances all shaped the crisis. Joanna’s shifting position and Charles of Durazzo’s ambitions made Naples an immediate security problem. Military defense and territorial recovery consumed money while papal taxation provoked resistance. Urban’s rigidity intensified these institutional and financial pressures, damaging the alliances on which the Roman obedience depended.

summary.text: Urban VI’s election in Rome was followed within months by a rival election and the Western Schism. A skilled administrator before becoming pope, he pursued reform with a confrontational style that alienated cardinals. His struggle with the Avignon obedience became entangled with the succession to Naples and violence against his own opponents.

paragraphs.text: Bartolomeo Prignano studied canon law, served in the Neapolitan Church and became an experienced official of the Avignon chancery. His reputation for ability and personal rigor made him an attractive candidate outside the College of Cardinals. The first conclave held in Rome after the return from Avignon took place amid intense popular demands for a Roman or Italian pope.

Cardinals initially recognized him, then challenged the election’s freedom and chose Robert of Geneva as Clement VII at Fondi. Urban maintained his own legitimacy. Later he replaced Joanna of Naples with Charles of Durazzo, but their alliance collapsed. During the ensuing struggle he imprisoned cardinals accused of plotting against him; torture and killings gravely damaged his government. His pontificate ended without reconciliation.

actions.text: Created new cardinals to sustain the Roman obedience after the rival election, institutionalizing a divided Church.
Planned a jubilee for 1390; the celebration would take place under his successor.

paragraphs.text: The dispute was not simply a quarrel between two personalities. Legal testimony about the conclave, the cardinals’ conception of their own authority, Roman civic pressure and princely alliances all shaped the crisis. Joanna’s shifting position and Charles of Durazzo’s ambitions made Naples an immediate security problem. Military defense and territorial recovery consumed money while papal taxation provoked resistance. Urban’s rigidity intensified these institutional and financial pressures, damaging the alliances on which the Roman obedience depended.

people.summary: Boniface IX strengthened the Roman papacy during the Western Schism but did not restore Church unity. He supported Ladislaus in Naples, recovered influence in the Papal States and ended much of Rome’s municipal independence. Pilgrimages and papal revenues sustained his government while rival obediences and pressure for mutual resignation persisted.
people.biography:
Pietro Tomacelli, from a Neapolitan noble family, rose through Urban VI’s cardinal appointments before his own election. His more conciliatory personal manner contrasted with Urban’s, but he defended the same Roman succession. He inherited a depleted chancery, scattered records and weak finances, alongside territories where communes, nobles and mercenary companies limited papal power.

Boniface backed Ladislaus against the Angevin claimant favored by Avignon and gradually rebuilt his position around Rome. He reinforced strategic strongholds and secured expanded authority over the city in 1398. Clement VII’s death did not end the schism: the Avignon cardinals chose Benedict XIII. Boniface rejected calls to resign together with his rival. The jubilee of 1400 nevertheless brought large numbers of pilgrims, including visitors from outside his regular obedience.

actions.text: Supported Ladislaus’s coronation and campaigns, tying the Roman obedience to the Neapolitan succession struggle.
Consolidated papal government in Rome and celebrated the 1400 jubilee despite plague and political insecurity.

people.context: The schism divided income as well as allegiance. The obediences had porous boundaries: bishops, cities and rulers could follow different claimants or exploit neutrality. Around Rome, rival-supported commanders and local lords obstructed communication and taxation. Boniface’s efforts to rebuild territorial power therefore depended on negotiation, military spending and revenues from ecclesiastical offices. Political recovery helped stabilize his own obedience but made surrendering the office less attractive, frustrating proposals that both claimants should step aside.

people.summary: Innocent VII inherited a divided Church and a capital in revolt. His legal and financial experience did not free him from dependence on King Ladislaus of Naples. The murder of Roman delegates by his nephew provoked flight to Viterbo, leaving plans for a council and reconciliation with the Avignon obedience unrealized.
people.biography:
Cosmato dei Migliorati began his career in the clergy of Sulmona and became a canon-law doctor, papal financial official and diplomat. Service as collector of English revenues and appointments at Ravenna and Bologna placed him inside the government of the Roman obedience. As cardinal he negotiated among northern Italian powers before being elected in 1404, after promising to work for an end to the schism.

Ladislaus initially helped arbitrate between the new pope and Rome’s competing factions. The settlement divided civic appointments and jurisdiction, but it did not remove the king’s territorial ambitions. In 1405 Ludovico Migliorati seized and killed members of a Roman delegation. The ensuing uprising drove Innocent and his court to Viterbo; papal apartments and archives were attacked. He returned in 1406 and challenged Ladislaus, but died before resolving the schism.

actions.text: Proposed a general council after pledging to seek unity, but Roman upheaval prevented the plan from producing a settlement.
Excommunicated Ladislaus after the king’s intervention became a threat to papal control rather than protection.

people.context: Colonna and Orsini competition intersected with the war between Ladislaus and the Angevin claimant to Naples. Rome’s communal government also contested who should guard bridges, choose officials and administer justice. Innocent therefore confronted a constitutional struggle inside the city as well as a Church divided between Rome and Benedict XIII. The assassination of delegates transformed negotiable disputes into a crisis of trust, while Ladislaus could present himself as mediator and exploit the resulting weakness.

people.summary: Gregory XII became pope with a promise to resign if that would reunite the Church. Negotiations failed, and the Council of Pisa’s rival election added a third obedience. His eventual resignation through representatives at Constance in 1415 provided a decisive step toward ending the Western Schism and electing Martin V.
people.biography:
Angelo Correr’s career was rooted in Venice. A theologian associated with Bologna, he became bishop of Castello and later titular Latin patriarch of Constantinople. Venetian support, fiscal responsibilities and curial service connected him to the Roman obedience. Elected in 1406, he publicly renewed the cardinals’ pledge to surrender the office if his rival also resigned and a united election could follow.

The proposed meeting with Benedict XIII at Savona collapsed amid distrust, family influence and political obstruction. Gregory’s creation of new cardinals intensified the rupture with dissident members of his own college. Pisa declared both rivals deposed and elected Alexander V in 1409, but neither accepted its judgment. At Constance, Gregory’s representatives formally authorized the council’s continuation and presented his resignation. He retained an honored ecclesiastical position and died before Martin V’s election.

actions.text: Negotiated, unsuccessfully, for mutual resignation with Benedict XIII; the failure helped drive cardinals toward Pisa.
Authorized action at Constance and resigned on 4 July 1415, removing the Roman claim without requiring his acceptance of deposition.

people.context: The schism made a bishop’s allegiance, revenue and jurisdiction depend on competing papal appointments. Correr had experienced those administrative pressures long before election. His Venetian kin supplied a trusted governing network, but their promotion also undermined confidence that he would sacrifice office for unity. Ladislaus feared a settlement favorable to France and the Angevin cause. Constance ultimately combined princely pressure, conciliar procedure and voluntary resignation rather than solving the crisis through a simple agreement between two men.
